# Writing and shaping notes {#sec-notes}

A musical note has several independent qualities: where it starts, how long
it lasts, its pitch and its velocities. The piano roll brings these together
visually. The editing grid supplies a musical ruler, while the inspector
provides exact values when a performance needs finer attention.

This chapter explains the difference between placing a cursor, creating a
note and changing a note. Keeping those actions separate makes it possible
to navigate through music without accidentally moving it.

Pitch names use C4 for MIDI note 60. Octave labels differ between sequencers;
the numeric pitch in the inspector gives an unambiguous comparison.

## The grid is a ruler

The **editing grid** is a track's time step. With an eighth-note grid, the
ordinary left and right movements visit eighth-note positions. `:grid 1/8`
sets that grid directly; `z` then Left (or `zh`) makes it finer, and `z`
then Right (or `zl`) coarser. Ctrl-T toggles
triplets. The `z` family also contains zoom commands, but grid and zoom are
different: the grid changes the musical step, while zoom changes how much
music fits on screen.

Changing the grid does not quantise existing notes. A note recorded slightly
late remains late, even if the new grid is coarse. This preserves the
performance while giving later edits a useful ruler. Tab visits existing
notes independently of that ruler, so off-grid material remains accessible.

Note fractions describe durations: `1/4` is a quarter note, `1/8` an eighth,
`1/8.` a dotted eighth and `1/8t` an eighth-note triplet. They describe musical
length, not elapsed seconds. The tempo determines how long they take to play.

## A default note belongs to the track

A new note needs a length and velocity before it exists. Each track therefore
has a **default note**, separate from the note under the cursor. The default
is a set of values for subsequent note entry; changing it leaves existing
notes alone.

`:len 1/8` fixes the default length at an eighth note. `:len grid` makes it
follow the editing grid instead. The Tracks view also exposes the track's
Grid, Length and Vel fields. `, n` takes the length and velocity of the
current note as the new defaults: an existing phrase can supply the values
for the next one.

In the piano roll, `o` adds the default note at the cursor's time and pitch.
`O` adds it and advances the cursor. By default that advance is the note's
length, which suits writing one note after another. With `gridadvance` on
(`, T g`), it is a grid step instead, useful for separated attacks or notes
whose lengths overlap in time at different pitches. A count repeats entry:
`8O` writes eight notes in succession.

The editor refuses to create an overlap with another note of the same pitch.
An imported performance may already contain such overlaps; Modal retains
that data, but ordinary entry and movement do not introduce new ones.

## Cursor movement and note movement

The ordinary arrow keys move the cursor, as do `h`, `j`, `k` and `l`.
Holding Alt with an arrow changes the intention to moving the note under
the cursor; the corresponding Alt-letter bindings are alternatives.
Adding Shift gives the finer time nudge or the larger pitch step shown below.
Pitch changes can be heard through **audition**:
a short playback of the current note as the cursor lands on it, a note is
added, or one note is moved to another pitch. Audition uses the track's output
and channel. It does not run while the song is playing or recording, or while
a Visual selection grows. `, T a` switches it on or off.

| Keys in the piano roll | Change |
| --- | --- |
| Alt-Left / Alt-Right, or `Alt-h` / `Alt-l` | Move the note to the previous / next grid line |
| Alt-Shift-Left / Alt-Shift-Right, or `Alt-H` / `Alt-L` | Nudge its start earlier / later in real time |
| `Alt-{` / `Alt-}` | Move it a bar earlier / later |
| Alt-Up / Alt-Down, or `Alt-k` / `Alt-j` | Move it up / down a semitone |
| Alt-Shift-Up / Alt-Shift-Down, or `Alt-K` / `Alt-J` | Move it up / down an octave |
| `=` / `-` | Move its end to the next / previous grid step |
| `+` / `_` | Lengthen / shorten it by a nudge |
| Ctrl-A / Ctrl-X | Increase / decrease its velocity |
| `x` / `Y` | Delete / yank the current note |

A **nudge** is a small time adjustment measured in milliseconds, initially
5 ms, controlled by `:set nudge=5`. It suits a performance adjustment whose
size should be independent of the tempo. Grid movement instead suits a
change in rhythmic position. Shift-Left and Shift-Right (or `H` and `L`),
without Alt, nudge the cursor;
this allows a new note to be placed between grid lines.

There is also a useful distinction between snapping and shifting. Alt-left
and Alt-right move notes onto neighbouring grid lines. The `t` and `T`
operators shift a target by a grid step while retaining each event's existing
offset from the grid. A phrase can therefore move by an eighth note without
losing its internal timing. In the piano roll those operators take notes;
in event-oriented views they can also move the other MIDI events with them.

## A selection remains the same music while it moves

The movement and length keys work on a Visual selection too. After movement,
the selection follows the notes it took: passing over an unselected note does
not collect it. This matters when moving a phrase through a busy passage.
The target remains the chosen phrase, rather than becoming whatever happens
to occupy its new rectangle.

A deliberate extension or a new object selects an area again. Escape ends
the selection, and `gv` recalls it. Repeated moves of the same kind within
an unchanged selection undo together; redefining or ending the selection
starts a separate gesture for subsequent moves.

A selected edit is refused as a whole if one of its notes would become
invalid, for example by moving before the song or overlapping another note
of its pitch. The message identifies the problem. This preserves the shape
of a phrase instead of moving only the notes that happen to fit.

## Timing in the inspector

The note inspector separates **Start**, **Length** and **Ends**. Start and
Ends are positions, counted from bar 1 and beat 1; Length is a duration.
Changing Ends changes the duration without moving the start.

Each timing row offers a coarse musical value, a signed fine adjustment in
**ticks**, and an exact value. Ticks are the song's small integer time units;
their musical size depends on its resolution. The coarse value gives an
accessible musical position while Fine preserves expressive timing near it.
A coarse edit keeps that fine remainder, rather than snapping the note.

The coarse unit normally follows the editing grid. `:set timingunit=1/16`
fixes the inspector's unit at a sixteenth note; `:set timingunit=grid`
restores grid-following. This is a display choice and does not move notes.

The note's release velocity, shown as Off Vel, is distinct from its attack
velocity. Instruments vary in how they respond to it; it can be inspected
and edited without changing the note's attack.

## Editing in the inspector {#sec-inspector-editing}

The inspector is also where a thing's details are changed. `e` opens it for
editing: here the note under the cursor, and elsewhere an event in the event
list, a section on the strip, a track's playback quantise and a controller
ramp. Every inspector is edited the same way, so what follows applies to all
of them.

An open inspector is best thought of as a **draft**. Each change is made at
once, so a note moved a few ticks can be seen in place and heard on the next
pass of a loop, but the changes are held together until you decide. Keeping
them makes the whole visit one undo step, however many fields changed; cancelling
puts everything back as it was when the inspector opened. The panel takes a
tint while it is being edited, and its values brighten, so a draft is never
left open unnoticed. Values that cannot be edited stay dim.

| In an open inspector | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Typing | Replace the current field's value |
| Enter | Set the field and stay on it, to adjust it again |
| Tab / Shift-Tab | Set the field and move to the next / previous one |
| Up / Down | Step the field's value, or its choice |
| Ctrl-Enter | Keep the draft, from any field |
| Escape | Put back what was typed; then cancel the draft |

Tab continues past the last field to two buttons at the panel's bottom
right, **Keep** and **Cancel**, where Enter presses the one chosen. They
appear only while editing. Ctrl-Enter is the quicker way to keep, from
wherever the cursor is.

Escape works in layers, undoing the most recent thing first. If a value has
been typed but not yet set, Escape restores the field. With nothing typed,
it cancels the draft, and every change since the inspector opened goes, with
nothing left to redo. Pressing Escape twice is therefore a reliable way out.

A field with a fixed set of choices is marked with a down arrow. Up and Down
step through its choices without opening anything, which is often enough.
Enter or Alt-Down opens its list to see them all; Enter there chooses one and
closes the list.

An inspector opens again on the field used last, which is useful when making
the same kind of adjustment to several notes in turn.

Editing a table's cell in place, as in the event list, Tracks and Ports, is a
different and smaller action: Enter sets that one value and leaves, and each
change is its own undo step. The inspector gathers several related values
into one decision; a table cell is a single value.

## Chords and the event list

For chord operations, Modal groups nearby note starts using `chordwindow`,
initially 30 ms. This recognises a played chord even when the fingers did not
land at exactly the same tick. The chord inspector identifies its notes and
velocities. `g` then Up or Down (or `gk` and `gj`) moves through its notes,
while `(` and `)` navigate
between chords. The `ic` object gives an operator the chord as a target.

The **event list** (`ge`) is useful when the grid conceals a distinction,
such as two events very close in time or a controller beside a note. Each
event is a row and its fields are columns. Enter edits the current field in
place; `e` opens the inspector on the whole event (@sec-inspector-editing).
Numeric steps and relative entries such as `+10`
allow an adjustment without retyping the full value.

The conductor's dim rows provide landmarks among a track's events. Tempo
and meter are edited in the conductor's own list (`gc`), rather than by
altering those contextual rows on a note track. The list and piano roll
are complementary views of the same stored performance.

## Seeing the right amount of music

`zi`, `zo` and `z0` zoom in, out and back to the normal scale. `zz` centres
the cursor. The piano roll shows pages of whole bars, keeping bar structure
legible as the scale changes. Page and half-page movements cover larger
distances; the compact key reference collects them in @sec-key-reference.

During playback, moving away from the playhead allows another passage to be
inspected. `zf` resumes following. Editing position and listening position
can remain separate for as long as the task needs them to be.
